strengths: Addresses a useful image-stitching problem: repairing local structural discontinuities that remain after alignment and seam cutting. Restricting additional alignment to problematic seam regions is a practical contribution.

The pipeline is intuitive and well illustrated. Dense patch alignment, spatial flow attenuation, and boundary-constrained seam merging form a coherent repair strategy, supported by pseudocode and several implementation parameters.

Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets. Figures 1, 7, and 11 demonstrate visible improvements in structural continuity. The selected user study reports 108 first-place votes for the proposed method, and runtime measurements indicate advantages over repeated seam estimation in difficult cases.
Established methods and public datasets are appropriately credited. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 provide useful, candid discussion of failures under substantial residual displacement.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution over existing seam-guided alignment is insufficiently established. SSIM-based seam evaluation is inherited from [17], and seam-guided local alignment is already central to [18]. Beyond Figure 4's qualitative sigmoid example, there are no systematic ablations isolating patch selection, flow attenuation, and seam-merging constraints. Experiments also use only alignment method [15] and initial seam method [16], leaving the claimed broad compatibility unverified.

Quantitative comparisons are restricted to seam-cutting methods [16,17]. The directly relevant seam-driven approaches [18,26] receive only selected qualitative comparisons, while other relevant approaches discussed in the manuscript, such as residual-based large-parallax stitching [12], are not evaluated. This limits evidence for the claimed advantage over existing large-parallax solutions.

The principal quantitative metric, Equation (5), closely follows the SSIM criterion used to identify repair regions and measures agreement along the seam rather than overall mosaic fidelity. It does not independently assess deformation or content preservation, and the manuscript itself identifies a disagreement with visual quality. The perceptual study helps, but uses only eight manually selected image groups without a sufficiently specified selection or randomization protocol. Table 1 also needs clarification: the baseline rank counts total 159 and 161 rather than the expected 160 each; this smaller reporting issue would not itself overturn the observed preference.

The central flow modification is incompletely specified. Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized spatial position, whereas the text and algorithm describe applying f to the displacement vector. The exact modified displacement mapping, treatment of general seam orientations, and handling of overlapping repair patches are unclear. These details materially affect reproducibility and the claimed smooth integration of patches.

The claim that the method can almost remove the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated operating regime: Section 3.4 assumes small residual parallax within patches, and Section 4.4 requires failures to remain localized. Furthermore, the acceptance rule max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts any constant error signal, including uniformly poor alignment such as Q = 0.8. Algorithm 1 also lacks a post-repair quality check. These issues weaken the reliability argument and the assertion that false-positive repairs cannot worsen results.
